This paper studies a timely and underexplored problem: how to obtain formal privacy guarantees for inference-time activation steering when the steering demonstrations are private. The core proposal, PSA, is simple and appealing: compute per-layer steering vectors from positive/negative demonstration pairs, clip the per-example activation differences, add Gaussian noise, and then use the privatized vectors for arbitrary downstream generations. The paper also introduces a membership inference attack tailored to activation editing using only generated text, and reports experiments across several alignment benchmarks and model families. Overall, I find the paper interesting and potentially impactful, especially because activation editing is increasingly used as a lightweight alternative to finetuning, yet its privacy implications have received little attention.

The main strength of the paper is conceptual clarity. The privacy mechanism is straightforward, easy to implement, and leverages standard DP tools in a setting where post-processing is especially attractive: once the noisy steering vectors are released, one can answer arbitrarily many queries without additional privacy cost. This is a meaningful systems-level advantage over many interactive private inference schemes. I also appreciate that the paper does not oversell novelty on the mechanism itself; the novelty is primarily in identifying activation steering as a privacy-sensitive alignment pipeline and adapting DP to it. That framing is valuable.

A second strength is breadth of empirical coverage. The paper evaluates multiple model families and several alignment-relevant behaviors, and includes not only benchmark accuracy but also open-ended generation quality and a check on general capabilities via MMLU. The scaling observation—that larger models appear to incur less utility degradation under the same privatization scheme—is plausible and practically relevant. The proposed text-only MIA is also a useful contribution, since logits are often unavailable in realistic black-box settings.

That said, I have several concerns, some of them substantial.

The most important issue is the precision and correctness of the DP accounting and mechanism specification. As written, Algorithm 1 clips each difference vector via
bar d_i^l = d_i^l / max{C_l, ||d_i^l||_2}.
This ensures norm at most 1/C_l when C_l > ||d_i^l||, or at most 1 when ||d_i^l|| > C_l, depending on interpretation; in any case it is not the standard clipping formula d_i * min(1, C_l / ||d_i||). The text says “project to an L2 ball of radius C_l and then scale by the same constant C_l,” but the equation does not match that description. If the intended output is bounded in norm by 1, then the sensitivity of the average under replace-one adjacency is at most 2/n, which matches the stated sigma. But then C_l disappears from the actual sensitivity and only affects whether small vectors are shrunk, which is unusual and likely undesirable. If instead the intended clipping radius is C_l, then sigma should scale with C_l. This discrepancy is central because it affects both the formal guarantee and the utility interpretation. The mechanism needs to be rewritten carefully and the sensitivity proof made explicit.

Relatedly, the Gaussian mechanism statement is dimensionally underspecified. The notation N(0, sigma^2) suggests scalar noise, but the steering vector is d-dimensional, so the mechanism should add isotropic Gaussian noise N(0, sigma^2 I_d). This is probably what the authors mean, but for a DP paper this should be stated precisely.

The privacy accounting across layers is also somewhat underdeveloped. The paper uses basic composition over selected layers and reports total epsilon as five times per-layer epsilon. That is acceptable, but only if each layer’s noisy vector is released independently with its own privacy budget. However, the same private examples are reused across layers, and the activations across layers are highly correlated. Basic composition still applies, but the paper should be explicit that the guarantee is with respect to joint release of all selected vectors and that the per-layer noise is calibrated accordingly. More importantly, the choice to fix the same noise standard deviation 0.02 across datasets and then back out epsilon is unusual from a DP perspective. Typically one fixes epsilon, delta and sensitivity, then derives sigma. Here the paper seems to fix sigma and report the implied epsilon, which is fine experimentally, but then comparisons across datasets and models become harder to interpret. It would be much stronger to present utility as a function of epsilon, not just for one chosen sigma.

A second major concern is the empirical evaluation methodology. The paper repeatedly claims “minimal loss in performance,” but the evidence is somewhat thin. Figure 3 is visually suggestive, yet there are no confidence intervals, no repeated runs over DP noise seeds, and no statistical tests. Since PSA injects randomness, variance matters. In some settings the paper even claims PSA outperforms non-private steering; without repeated trials this could simply be noise. At minimum, the authors should report mean and standard deviation over multiple noise draws and, ideally, multiple random subsets of demonstrations if applicable.

The open-ended generation evaluation is also not very convincing in its current form. Table 3 reports GPT-4 scores, but the scale is hard to interpret and many absolute values look odd, especially for behaviors like sycophancy and AI coordination where all methods score near zero or one. It is unclear whether higher is always better in the same sense across behaviors, what exact rubric GPT-4 used, and whether these scores reflect alignment success, helpfulness, or textual quality. The paper says the prompts are in the appendix, but the main text should summarize the rubric and discuss evaluator reliability. Given the sensitivity of LLM-as-a-judge results, some human validation or at least agreement checks would strengthen the claims.

The MMLU evaluation is similarly hard to assess because Table 5 appears incomplete or malformed: the zero-shot row is truncated, and only one value is shown. More broadly, converting MMLU to A/B format and averaging probability of the correct answer is nonstandard enough that more detail is needed. Since steering is applied globally at inference time, one might expect behavior-specific vectors to affect unrelated tasks in subtle ways; a fuller capability evaluation would be useful.

The membership inference attack is interesting, but I am not fully convinced it measures what the paper claims. The attack inserts synthetic canaries into demonstrations and then tests whether the steered model prefers the target canary when prompted with the anchor canary. This is closer to a targeted memorization or influence probe than a generic membership inference attack on natural examples. That is not necessarily a problem, but the paper should be more careful in terminology and scope. The attack demonstrates that steering vectors can encode and reveal rare inserted associations; it does not yet show broad membership leakage for arbitrary private demonstrations. Also, the threshold tau is chosen differently for different models, apparently heuristically, and the attack uses 100 generations at temperature 0.8. The sensitivity of results to tau, temperature, decoding strategy, and number of samples should be reported. Otherwise the empirical epsilon estimates may be fragile.

On empirical epsilon, the paper should be more cautious. Computing an “empirical epsilon” from one attack’s FPR/FNR is a lower bound on privacy loss under that attack class, not a direct estimate of the mechanism’s true privacy parameter. The text sometimes reads as if lower empirical epsilon means “stronger protection in real-world settings” in a broad sense. That is too strong. It only means the specific attack did not exploit the full available leakage. This distinction matters.

I also found some inconsistencies and presentation issues that reduce confidence. The abstract says experiments on models from 0.5B to 7B and “different sizes and model families,” but the main model list in Section 5.1 names four models, while the scaling section later introduces additional Qwen sizes. The abstract says “seven different benchmarks,” but these are really seven behavioral datasets from a common benchmark suite. There are several typographical artifacts and formatting errors, including stray footnote markers (“111”, “222”, etc.), malformed algorithm text, and the incomplete MMLU table. These are fixable, but in a privacy paper, sloppiness around equations and tables is more concerning than usual.

There are also some missing baselines and ablations. Since the method is essentially noisy mean steering after clipping, I would like to see at least: a non-private clipped mean steering baseline to isolate the effect of clipping from noise; an ablation over number and choice of steered layers; an ablation over clipping threshold C_l; and a privacy-utility curve over sigma or epsilon. It would also be useful to compare against a simple private alternative such as using a small public dataset for steering or using DP selection of a subset of demonstrations, if feasible. For the MIA, comparing against attacks on logits when available would help contextualize the difficulty of the text-only setting.

One conceptual question is the adjacency notion. The paper says neighboring datasets differ in one record, where a record is a paired demonstration (p_i, c_i^+, c_i^-). That is reasonable, but in some applications privacy may need to protect all data associated with one user, potentially multiple demonstrations. Group privacy would then worsen epsilon. The paper should at least discuss this limitation. Similarly, if prompts themselves are sensitive, the threat model should clarify whether the released steering vectors could leak prompt content as well as completion content; the current exposition focuses more on completions.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has a solid core idea and addresses an important gap. The main novelty is not a new DP mechanism per se, but the formulation of private activation steering and the demonstration that offline privatization of steering vectors can preserve much of the utility. If the DP mechanism is corrected and the empirical evaluation is tightened, this could become a strong contribution.

My recommendation is borderline positive to weak reject in its current form, depending on the conference bar for methodological rigor in privacy papers. I lean slightly negative because the clipping/noise specification and sensitivity accounting are too ambiguous for a paper whose central claim is formal DP guarantees. If those issues are merely exposition mistakes and the underlying implementation is correct, then the paper would improve substantially.

The most important revisions I would ask for are: first, correct and fully specify the clipping rule, sensitivity proof, and Gaussian mechanism in vector form; second, report results over multiple DP noise seeds with uncertainty estimates; third, provide privacy-utility curves as a function of epsilon and ablations on clipping threshold and number of layers; fourth, clarify the scope of the MIA and present robustness analyses for tau, temperature, and decoding; and fifth, fix the presentation issues, especially the malformed tables and algorithm descriptions.

In summary, this is a promising and relevant paper with a nice problem formulation and a practical approach, but the current version falls short on the rigor needed to substantiate its formal privacy claims and some of its empirical conclusions.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies privacy-preserving activation steering for LLM alignment. It proposes PSA, which computes per-layer steering vectors from paired positive/negative demonstrations, clips the per-example activation differences, adds Gaussian noise, and then uses the privatized vectors during inference-time activation editing. The authors claim formal differential privacy guarantees for the private demonstration set, no additional privacy cost for unlimited downstream queries by post-processing, and empirically small utility loss relative to non-private mean steering across several alignment benchmarks, GPT-4 judged open-ended generation, and MMLU. The paper also introduces a canary-based membership inference attack tailored to activation steering and reports reduced attack success under PSA.
strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem: privacy risks of inference-time activation steering rather than training/fine-tuning.
The core idea is simple and practically appealing: privatize a small set of steering vectors offline, then reuse them for arbitrary future queries.
Provides a clear DP framing and leverages standard Gaussian mechanism and post-processing arguments to motivate unlimited-query deployment once the privatized vectors are released.
Evaluates across multiple model families, sizes, and several alignment-related behaviors, which gives some breadth to the empirical study.
Introduces a steering-specific black-box canary-based membership inference attack, which is a useful empirical auditing contribution.
Findings suggest that larger models may better absorb DP noise, an interesting empirical observation for privacy-utility tradeoffs.
weaknesses: The DP mechanism and its presentation contain important ambiguities/inconsistencies, especially around clipping, sensitivity, and noise calibration.

The clipping formula in Algorithm 1 appears mathematically incorrect for projection to an L2 ball of radius C_l; as written it scales vectors to norm at most 1/C_l rather than clipping to radius C_l, which undermines the stated sensitivity analysis.

Noise is described inconsistently: Algorithm 1 gives sigma determined by epsilon, delta, and n, while the experiments state a fixed Gaussian noise standard deviation of 0.02 and then derive epsilon values. It is unclear whether the mechanism is truly calibrated per layer/dataset or fixed heuristically.

The privacy accounting is simplistic and potentially misleading. The paper uses basic composition over layers only, but does not carefully discuss whether layer selection, hyperparameter tuning, threshold selection, or use of any private validation data incurs additional privacy cost.
Empirical evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, variance across random seeds/noise draws, or significance testing are reported for the main utility results.
The GPT-4 evaluation is weakly informative and in some cases the reported scores are extremely low or close to zero, making the interpretation of text quality and behavioral success unclear.
The MIA is highly specialized to synthetic canaries and threshold tuning, so it is not clear how well it reflects realistic privacy leakage from steering vectors on natural private data.
Claims of 'minimal loss in performance' are not always convincingly supported because several reported gains/losses are small, noisy-looking, and not accompanied by uncertainty estimates.
Some tables/experimental reporting appear incomplete or inconsistent (e.g., Table 5 seems truncated/incomplete for zero-shot MMLU).

The paper occasionally overstates conclusions, e.g., suggesting empirical epsilon being lower than theoretical epsilon means stronger real-world protection, despite the attack being only one lower-bound style audit and not a comprehensive privacy characterization.
methodological_flaws: Algorithm 1's clipping/scaling equation is likely wrong. For clipping to radius C_l, the standard form is d_i^l / max(1, ||d_i^l||_2 / C_l) or equivalently C_l d_i^l / max(C_l, ||d_i^l||_2). The paper instead uses d_i^l / max(C_l, ||d_i^l||_2), which does not implement the claimed projection and changes sensitivity by an extra factor of 1/C_l. This is a substantive mathematical flaw because the DP proof depends on correct sensitivity bounds.

The stated Gaussian noise calibration sigma = 2*sqrt(2 ln(1.25/delta)) / (n epsilon) implicitly assumes per-example contribution norm bounded by 1 and neighboring datasets differing by replacement, giving sensitivity 2/n. But this only matches the flawed normalization if C_l <= 1 or if vectors are normalized to unit norm; otherwise the sensitivity derivation is not justified. The proof sketch omits these assumptions.

The paper claims the mechanism outputs are (|S| epsilon, |S| delta)-DP for selected layers, but if the same private examples are used to tune C_l, choose layers, choose lambda, or select the best-performing setup, privacy composition should include those steps unless done on public data. This is not rigorously established.

The empirical privacy evaluation computes an 'empirical epsilon' from one attack's FPR/FNR. This quantity is at best a lower bound on distinguishability under that specific adversary, not an estimate of the true privacy parameter of the mechanism. Interpreting smaller empirical epsilon than theoretical epsilon as evidence of stronger real-world privacy is scientifically overstated.

The MIA threshold tau is manually chosen per model, which may leak attack-side tuning assumptions and can materially affect FPR/FNR. The paper does not specify whether threshold selection used held-out trials, nor how robust results are to tau.

The utility experiments do not report variability over DP noise realizations. Since PSA is randomized, single-run comparisons can be misleading; averaging over multiple privatized vectors is necessary for valid empirical claims.

The comparison to non-private PCA steering is not fully fair conceptually because PSA privatizes mean steering only; there is no private analogue of PCA steering, and the rationale for excluding stronger/private baselines is limited.

The claim that advanced composition is looser than basic composition for fewer than 5 layers is not generally justified as stated; tighter accounting depends on the exact accountant and parameters. This is a minor but notable imprecision in scientific logic.
